newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian bonds open stronger on Greenspan speech.
newsitem.headline: Canadian bonds open stronger on Greenspan speech.

text.p: Canadian bonds opened stronger in active trade on Friday, outperforming U.S. Treasuries, after comments from U.S. Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan were interpreted as bullish for bonds.

"Rightly or wrongly, it's the market's interpretation of Greenspan's speech last night. I think it's wrong, but a lot of people are reading it as saying basically he's softening his stance," said Sheldon Dong, manager of fixed income research with Midland Walwyn Capital Inc.
Canada's 30-year benchmark bond rose C$0.68 to C$110.63 to yield 7.098 percent.
The U.S. 30-year bond rose 20/32 to yield 6.88 percent. The spread between the two bonds widened to 22 basis points from 23 basis points at Thursday's close.
Greenspan said in a speech on Thursday he expects economic growth to slow later this year and into next, but added that the central bank would need to act if that does not prove to be the case.

The speech prompted a rally in both Canadian and U.S. fixed-income markets, and helped the Canadian dollar strengthen against the U.S. currency. Many traders believe the speech rules out a May 20 rate hike by the Fed.

In other news, Statistics Canada, in its last such release before the June 2 federal election, said on Friday the unemployment rate rose to 9.6 percent in April from 9.3 percent in March. Analysts said the news did not have a major impact on bond prices.
In other prices, Canada's 10-year benchmark bond rose C$0.73 to C$103.30 to yield 6.529 percent. The U.S. bond rose 18/32 to yield 6.66 percent.
The negative spread between the two bonds widened to 13 basis points from 10 basis points at the close of trading on Thursday.
The three-month cash T-bill traded with a yield of 3.04 percent against its U.S. equivalent which yielded 5.17 percent.
